facts.statement: Kairuku fossils date to 27 million years ago and were found in the Kokoamu Greensand Formation of New Zealand.
facts.quote: This taxon is known from bones from 27 MYA (late Oligocene), from the Kokoamu Greensand Formation of New Zealand.

facts.statement: The first Kairuku bones were discovered in 1977 by Ewan Fordyce, though they were not identified as Kairuku at that time.
facts.quote: The first Kairuku bones were discovered in 1977 by Ewan Fordyce, although they were not identified as such at the time.

facts.statement: In February 2012, a team led by Fordyce and Daniel Ksepka reconstructed a K. grebneffi skeleton using specimens from the Kokoamu Greensand of New Zealand.
facts.quote: In February 2012, an international team of scientists led by Fordyce and Daniel Ksepka reconstructed a K. grebneffi skeleton using a few "key specimens" from the Kokoamu Greensand of the North Otago and South Canterbury districts of New Zealand.

facts.statement: The holotype of K. grebneffi was collected in 1991 from the Waipati stream drainage area in New Zealand.
facts.quote: The holotype of K. grebneffi was collected in 1991 from a drainage area of the Waipati stream, a tributary of the Maerewhenua River.

facts.statement: Fossils of K. waewaeroa, known as the Kawhia giant penguin, were found in Kawhia Harbour on New Zealand's North Island.
facts.quote: Fossil remains of Kairuku waewaeroa, or Kawhia giant penguin, fossil remains were found in Kawhia Harbour on the North Island of New Zealand.

facts.statement: The genus name Kairuku is derived from the Māori words for 'food' and 'to dive'.
facts.quote: The genus name Kairuku comes from the Māori words kai ("food") and ruku ("to dive").

facts.statement: The species name waewaeroa comes from Māori words meaning 'long legs', referring to the bird's elongated hind limbs.
facts.quote: The species name waewaeroa is from Māori waewae - "legs", and roa - "long", referring to the elongated hind limbs.

facts.statement: K. grebneffi stood 1.28 meters tall, while K. waewaeroa could reach a height of 1.38 meters.
facts.quote: K. grebneffi stood 1.28 m tall, and K. waewaeroa is even larger with height up to 1.38 m.

facts.statement: K. grebneffi possesses the longest humerus bone of any penguin known from either the fossil record or living species.
facts.quote: K. grebneffi had the longest humerus bone of any penguin extant or attested to in the fossil record.

facts.statement: K. grebneffi had a longer bill and a more slender body compared to living penguin species.
facts.quote: The bird had a longer bill and more slender body compared to living penguins.

facts.statement: Relative to its body size, K. grebneffi had flippers that were longer and likely more flexible than those of extant penguin species.
facts.quote: Relative to its body size, its flippers were longer and probably more flexible than those of extant species.

facts.statement: Predators of K. grebneffi likely included sharks and Squalodons.
facts.quote: Predators of the bird likely included sharks and Squalodons.

facts.statement: K. grebneffi lived in what is now New Zealand during the late Oligocene, roughly 25 to 27 million years ago.
facts.quote: K. grebneffi lived in what is now New Zealand late in the Oligocene period, roughly 25–27 million years ago.

facts.statement: During the late Oligocene, the area now known as New Zealand consisted mostly of ocean with a few isolated islands.
facts.quote: At the time, most of the area was ocean, with a few isolated islands.

facts.statement: Researchers believe that rock outcrops provided safe breeding grounds and access to rich food resources for K. grebneffi.
facts.quote: It is believed that these rock outcrops provided safe breeding grounds and easy access to rich food resources in the surrounding seas.

facts.statement: Kairuku was historically classified under the genus Palaeeudyptes.
facts.quote: It was historically referred to as Palaeeudyptes.

facts.statement: The genus Kairuku was described by Ksepka, Fordyce, Ando & Jones in 2012.
